archetype.name: Game Manager (backup, play-action)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup asked to operate a run-first, defense-led offense on time. He takes the short, structured throws, feeds his top receiver and avoids the mistakes that have dogged his career.

report.headline: Two clean, efficient games that his career says won't last
report.take:
Drew Lock's 2026 is two appearances and 48 attempts of the best football he has ever played, and the context matters as much as the numbers. He arrives as an eighth-year journeyman whose career CPOE has been negative in every season on file, from -0.8 to -6.1. Over five prior seasons he never finished better than 15th in EPA per play, and he threw 15 interceptions in his one full-time year. This season he ranks 2nd of 43 in EPA per dropback (0.451), 4th in CPOE (+6.7) and 2nd in adjusted net yards per dropback, with no interceptions and no turnover-worthy plays. The depth chart now lists him as QB2 and he is questionable with a forearm injury. The dossier's start log and its game log don't fully agree on how many games he has started. Treat him as a backup with a hot two-game sample, not a quarterback who has taken the job.

The how is more convincing than the how much. Seattle runs this offense through its defense, which ranks 2nd in EPA allowed, and through a pass rate 5.7 points below expected. Lock has been asked to be efficient, not to carry it. His intended air yards sit at 7.7, he throws 1.25 yards short of the sticks on average, and his aggressiveness is 16.7%. Most of his damage came from structure. Under center he completed all 14 attempts with 0.891 EPA per play, which points to play-action and defined reads. From shotgun he was ordinary: 0.262 EPA, a 37% success rate and CPOE below expected. He has also leaned hard on one target. Jaxon Smith-Njigba drew 21 of his 48 throws and returned 1.178 EPA per target. Rashid Shaheed's eight targets were a loss (-0.451).

The numbers hide how small and soft the sample is. The Week 2 rout came against Arizona, now 29th in defensive EPA, and that one game supplied 16.1 of his 22.5 passing EPA. The deep line (1.971 EPA on five attempts) and the under-center perfection are a handful of plays each. His red-zone work (55.6% completions, -6.3 CPOE) is already more like the career version. His pocket also isn't protected: Seattle's line ranks 29th in hit rate allowed, and he has been hit or sacked on 16% of dropbacks.

If he plays again, expect a version that is still careful with the ball but much closer to his career baseline. That means a completion rate in the low 60s and EPA around average, propped up by play-action and Smith-Njigba rather than by a new level of accuracy. The ball security is the most plausible part to carry over, because it comes from the conservative design. The accuracy is the least plausible, because six seasons say otherwise.

strengths.title: Clean operation inside a structured offense
strengths.body: He has no interceptions and no turnover-worthy plays on 51 dropbacks, which ranks 1st in both INTs and INT rate. That is a product of the design: short targets, throws underneath the sticks and a run-heavy script. It is a sharp reversal from a career that included 15 picks in 2020. Because the conservative approach is the cause, some of it should hold, but a zero won't.

strengths.title: Lethal from under center
strengths.body: Under center he went 14 for 14 at 0.891 EPA per play, an 80% success rate and a CPOE of nearly 30. That is play-action and defined reads working in a run-first Macdonald offense. The edge is real in the sense that the scheme creates easy throws. Perfection on 15 plays is not repeatable.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba pays
strengths.body: Smith-Njigba drew 21 targets and produced 1.178 EPA per target, which accounts for most of Lock's efficiency. Leaning on the best receiver is sound quarterbacking. It also means the production depends on that receiver being healthy.

concerns.title: Accuracy far outside his career
concerns.body: His +6.7 CPOE ranks 4th. Every season on his record shows negative CPOE, including -6.1 in 2024 and -5.5 in his one full-time year. A two-game, 48-attempt jump with no change in his own profile is most likely noise plus soft throws, so expect heavy regression.

concerns.title: Backup status and forearm injury
concerns.body: The depth chart lists him as QB2 as of October 13, and he is questionable with a forearm injury after a limited practice. Whatever the reason for the demotion, his volume going forward is uncertain. A forearm problem on his throwing side would also cloud his accuracy.

concerns.title: Sample inflated by Arizona
concerns.body: His Week 2 passing EPA of 16.1 came against a defense now ranked 29th, while the Week 1 game against the 15th-ranked defense was a modest 187 yards. The deep production rests on five attempts. The red-zone numbers (-6.3 CPOE, 33% success) already look like his old self.

trend.note: Efficiency climbed from Week 1 (6.4 passing EPA against New England) to Week 2 (16.1 at Arizona), though the opponent explains much of the jump. He has since been listed as the backup.

nextGame.headline: Thursday at Denver: strong pass defense missing both starting corners
nextGame.body:
Denver's pass defense ranks 3rd in EPA and 4th against deep throws, so the downfield shots that flattered Lock's line are unlikely to be there. The opening is underneath. The Broncos rank 24th in short-pass EPA allowed, and running backs draw 24.3% of targets against them versus a league share of 18.2%. That suits a quarterback who lives at 7.7 intended air yards. Denver's run defense ranks 28th, which should feed the play-action looks he thrives on. Seattle's run game is 30th in EPA without Zach Charbonnet, though, so that is a theoretical edge more than a proven one.

Availability drives this game. Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss, both regular starters at corner, are out, and safety Talanoa Hufanga is questionable after not practicing. That is a real weakening of a top-three pass defense. On Seattle's side, Lock himself is questionable with a forearm injury and listed as QB2. Smith-Njigba, who drew 21 of his 48 throws, is questionable with an ankle injury. Rookie guard Beau Stephens is questionable on a line already 29th in hit rate. It is also a short week, four days of rest for a road Thursday game. Seattle is favored by 2.5 with a total of 40.5.

keyMatchups.title: Short passing game against soft underbelly
keyMatchups.body: Denver allows 0.129 EPA on short throws, 24th in the league, while Lock has posted 0.524 EPA on throws of 0-9 air yards. This is the clearest path to efficiency for a conservative passer. It holds even with a healthy Broncos secondary, because it reflects their coverage approach.

keyMatchups.title: Both Denver starting corners out
keyMatchups.body: With Surtain and Moss out, Denver's 3rd-ranked pass defense is playing well below the level its numbers were built on. If Smith-Njigba plays, he faces depth corners rather than the starters. This is the single biggest factor working in Seattle's passing game's favor.

keyMatchups.title: Smith-Njigba's ankle
keyMatchups.body: Lock's efficiency has run through one receiver. The next most-targeted receiver, Shaheed, has been a net negative. If Smith-Njigba is limited, the target tree thins out fast.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock is even active and starting. If he is, watch how often Seattle gets him under center for play-action against a short-handed Denver secondary.

restOfSeason.body:
As currently listed, Lock is a backup, so his rest-of-season value depends on whether and when he plays. If he starts, the conservative design should keep his turnovers low and his sack rate manageable. Expect the accuracy and per-play efficiency to fall well back toward a career in which he has never posted positive CPOE. The run-first approach (26th in pass rate over expected) caps his volume, and the 29th-ranked protection caps how long plays can develop.

The realistic projection as a starter is a game manager throwing for about 180-230 yards on 25-30 attempts, with EPA around league average rather than near the top. His floor will lean heavily on Smith-Njigba's health and on Seattle's defense creating short fields.
swingFactors: Whether he regains the starting job or stays QB2

confidence.note: The sample is 48 attempts, his production clashes with six seasons of career data, he is listed as QB2 and he is injured.
